common_name: Rocha Pear (Pêra Rocha, Portuguese PDO Pear)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees while dormant in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained loam in full sun; Rocha was first propagated near Sintra in the early 19th century and now carries Protected Designation of Origin status tied to the Oeste region west of Lisbon.

directions: Provide a compatible pollinizer and train on a central-leader or espalier system in deep, well-drained soil, since Rocha sets heavily and benefits from thinning for fruit size. Unlike buttery European pears, Rocha ripens to a dense, crisp, almost apple-like texture that holds its shape well in cooking while still turning sweet and aromatic, which is part of why it became Portugal's dominant pear export. Pick while the skin is still predominantly green with a faint golden blush and finish ripening in cool storage, where the fruit develops its characteristic fine-grained flesh and light floral fragrance over several weeks. Rocha accounts for the large majority of Portugal's pear orchards and is eaten fresh, in tarts, or poached in local wine.
sources: European Commission eAmbrosia Geographical Indications Register — Pêra Rocha do Oeste
Associação Nacional de Produtores de Pêra Rocha (ANP Rocha)
Instituto Nacional de Investigação Agrária e Veterinária (INIAV), Portugal

common_name: Elvas Plum (Ameixa de Elvas, Candied Greengage)
scientific_name: Prunus domestica 'Rainha Cláudia Verde de Elvas'

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, alkaline-leaning soil in full sun; this small greengage-type plum is grown around Elvas in the Alentejo and carries Protected Designation of Origin status for its traditional candied form.

directions: Pick the small yellow-green fruit while still firm rather than fully soft, since the Elvas tradition is to poach the plums whole in sugar syrup over repeated days until they turn translucent and glisten, a candying method documented in the Alentejo since at least the 19th century. The tree bears reliably in warm, dry summers typical of inland southern Portugal and tolerates poor, stony soils better than most plum types. Fresh-eaten fruit is tart and green-fleshed in the greengage style, but almost the entire Elvas crop is diverted into the candied 'ameixa de Elvas doce' sold in wooden boxes as a regional delicacy. Thin fruit clusters in late spring to improve the size and uniformity of plums destined for candying.
sources: European Commission eAmbrosia Geographical Indications Register — Ameixa de Elvas
Direção-Geral de Agricultura e Desenvolvimento Rural (DGADR), Portugal

common_name: Fundão Cherry (Cereja do Fundão, Cova da Beira Cherry)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter on a dwarfing rootstock in well-drained, granite-derived soil in full sun; this is the leading sweet cherry grown under the Cereja do Fundão/Cova da Beira Protected Geographical Indication in Portugal's mountainous Beira Interior.

directions: Site trees at elevation on well-drained granite or schist soils, which the Fundão region's high-altitude orchards rely on for the cool nights that sharpen the fruit's sugar-acid balance. Saco is a firm-fleshed, dark-red, late-ripening type among several traditional varieties grown under the regional designation, prized for holding its texture both fresh and when exported. Every spring, the blossoming orchards around Fundão draw visitors for the region's cherry blossom festival, and the fruit is picked by hand in June once it reaches full color to avoid splitting. Net or otherwise protect ripening fruit from birds and sudden rain, both of which quickly damage the thin-skinned cherries right before harvest.
sources: European Commission eAmbrosia Geographical Indications Register — Cereja do Fundão/Cova da Beira
Município do Fundão, Portugal

common_name: Aljezur Sweet Potato (Batata Doce de Aljezur)

planting.note: Plant rooted slips two to four weeks after the last frost into loose, sandy soil ridged for drainage in full sun; this landrace is grown along Portugal's southwest Atlantic coast around Aljezur and carries Protected Geographical Indication status.

directions: Grow in the loose, mineral-rich sandy soils that give this variety its name recognition, since Aljezur's coastal Costa Vicentina microclimate and sand-dune soils are credited with producing an unusually sweet, fragrant tuber compared to sweet potatoes grown on heavier inland soils. Vines sprawl vigorously across the sandy beds and should be hilled lightly as tubers swell, with minimal irrigation needed once established thanks to the region's mild, humid Atlantic air. Local smallholders have grown this landrace for generations, and the town celebrates it each November with a dedicated sweet potato festival. Dig before the first autumn frost, then cure the tubers at warm temperatures and high humidity for one to two weeks to concentrate their sweetness before storing.
sources: European Commission eAmbrosia Geographical Indications Register — Batata Doce de Aljezur

common_name: Azores Pineapple (Ananás dos Açores, São Miguel Greenhouse Pineapple)

planting.note: Plant a rooted crown or sucker in free-draining, humus-rich volcanic soil inside a greenhouse or warm, bright structure; this Protected Designation of Origin pineapple is traditionally grown in unheated glasshouses on São Miguel island in the Azores rather than outdoors.

directions: Unlike most commercial pineapples, the Azores crop is grown year-round under glass because the islands' mild but cool, overcast oceanic climate otherwise lacks the sustained heat pineapples need; growers traditionally smoulder small fires inside the greenhouses to trigger smoke-induced flowering rather than relying on tropical day-length and temperature cues. The slow, roughly two-year cycle in mineral-rich volcanic soil produces a notably small, intensely fragrant fruit with a tender, almost fully edible core and a tangier, more floral flavor than tropical field-grown pineapples. Harvest once the fruit's base turns from green to golden, and expect a far smaller yield per plant than tropical outdoor production, which is why this fruit commands a premium price. The tradition is centered on São Miguel, where family-run glasshouses have cultivated pineapple commercially since the 19th century.
sources: European Commission eAmbrosia Geographical Indications Register — Ananás dos Açores/São Miguel
Direção Regional da Agricultura e Desenvolvimento Rural, Açores

common_name: Bravo de Esmolfe Apple (Portuguese Heirloom Dessert Apple)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Bravo de Esmolfe is an old Beira Alta heirloom apple, named for the village of Esmolfe near Nelas, and carries Protected Designation of Origin status.

directions: Grow on a disease-resistant rootstock and keep the canopy open, as this heirloom is a lighter, more irregular bearer than modern commercial apples and benefits from good air circulation. The small-to-medium fruit ripens to a dull golden skin faintly blushed and speckled with russet, and is prized less for looks than for its dense, crisp flesh and an intense, almost spicy aromatic perfume that is widely considered among the finest of any Portuguese apple. Harvest in October once the fruit separates easily from the spur, and store it through the winter holidays, when it has traditionally been served on the Portuguese Christmas table. Commercial plantings remain small because the tree is a modest, inconsistent producer compared to modern cultivars, which has kept Bravo de Esmolfe a specialty rather than a supermarket apple.
sources: European Commission eAmbrosia Geographical Indications Register — Maçã Bravo de Esmolfe
Associação de Produtores de Maçã Bravo de Esmolfe

common_name: Riscadinha de Palmela Apple (Striped Portuguese Heirloom Apple)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in light, well-drained soil in full sun; this old apple from the Setúbal Peninsula town of Palmela carries Protected Designation of Origin status and is named for its fine, candy-cane-like red stripes.

directions: Site trees in the sandy, Mediterranean-climate soils around Palmela that the variety has been grown in for generations, where mild coastal winters still provide enough chill for reliable fruit set. The small, round apple has pale yellow-green skin finely streaked with narrow carmine-red stripes, giving rise to its diminutive name ('riscadinha' meaning 'little striped one'), and the flesh is crisp, juicy, and mildly aromatic rather than strongly flavored. Numbers declined sharply through the 20th century as growers shifted to higher-yielding modern varieties, and the apple survived mainly in old dooryard orchards before local producer associations began reviving it. Pick in early autumn once the stripes deepen to full color, and use promptly, as this heirloom is better suited to fresh eating than long storage.
sources: European Commission eAmbrosia Geographical Indications Register — Maçã Riscadinha de Palmela
Município de Palmela, Portugal

common_name: Óbidos Sour Cherry (Ginja de Óbidos, Ginjinha Cherry)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; this small sour cherry is grown around Óbidos and Alcobaça in the Oeste region and is the traditional base for Portugal's ginjinha liqueur, carrying Protected Geographical Indication status.

directions: This cherry is bred for acidity and aromatic intensity rather than fresh eating, producing small, deep-red to near-black fruit that is far too tart to enjoy straight off the tree. Growers around Óbidos, a walled medieval hill town, have long steeped the whole fruit in aguardente (grape brandy) with sugar and cinnamon to produce ginjinha, a sweet cherry liqueur traditionally served in a small chocolate cup with a cherry dropped in the bottom. Harvest by hand in June when the fruit is fully dark and before birds take the small, soft crop, since the thin skin bruises easily. Trees tolerate colder winters than sweet cherry types and need little pruning beyond removing dead or crossing wood, making this a relatively low-maintenance orchard tree once established.
sources: European Commission eAmbrosia Geographical Indications Register — Ginja de Óbidos e Alcobaça
Município de Óbidos, Portugal
Direção-Geral de Agricultura e Desenvolvimento Rural (DGADR), Portugal
